prompt: A page loads 20 resources over a single HTTP/2 connection on TCP. One segment carrying part of a JavaScript file is lost. What happens to the other 19 resources' data that arrives just after it?

options.text: It waits in the receiver's TCP buffer until the lost segment is retransmitted, because TCP delivers bytes strictly in order
options.explanation: Correct. TCP doesn't know about HTTP/2 streams; it only sees one byte stream, and it can't deliver later bytes past a hole. This is transport-level head-of-line blocking.

options.text: It is delivered immediately; only the JavaScript stream waits
options.explanation: QUIC removes the requirement for a stream to wait solely for another stream’s missing bytes. Shared flow control, congestion control and application dependencies can still delay delivery. TCP uses one ordered byte stream.

options.text: It is discarded and must be resent too
options.explanation: Out-of-order data can be retained and reported with SACK when negotiated. Receivers can also discard buffered data, so retention is not an unconditional guarantee.

options.text: The browser opens a new connection for the remaining resources
options.explanation: TCP handles this gap on the existing connection. The supplied scenario does not imply that the browser opens a replacement connection; doing so would require application-level recovery logic.

workedExample: HTTP/2 frames share TCP byte ordering. Later bytes cannot be delivered past the missing range until it is recovered; data already delivered is unaffected. Recovery duration is not fixed at one RTT. QUIC removes this cross-stream byte-order dependency, but shared congestion control, flow control and application dependencies can still delay multiple streams.

prompt: Which mechanisms can make transport extensions harder to deploy or help QUIC evolve? Select all that apply.

options.text: Some middleboxes interfere with unfamiliar TCP options or SYN data
options.explanation: Correct. Compatibility and fallback matter; this is not a claim that every middlebox behaves this way.

options.text: A TCP change in a kernel stack can depend on OS deployment cycles; a QUIC library can be updated with an application
options.explanation: Correct. Some TCP changes are sender-only, and neither TCP nor QUIC is required to live exclusively in one implementation layer.

options.text: Protecting QUIC control frames and selected header fields reduces the information middleboxes can depend on
options.explanation: Correct. Some wire fields remain visible and Initial keys are publicly derivable, so encryption does not eliminate all ossification or interference.

options.text: The TCP header has no room for any options
options.explanation: The base TCP header allows up to 40 option bytes. That finite space can constrain extensions too, but it is not zero; unfamiliar-option handling by middleboxes is a separate deployment obstacle.

options.text: The IETF has forbidden new TCP extensions since QUIC was standardised
options.explanation: TCP is still being extended (for example RACK-TLP in 2021 and AccECN, RFC 9768, in 2026). Deployment, not permission, is the barrier.

workedExample: The first three describe compatibility, implementation deployment and protection mechanisms. The base TCP header permits up to 40 option bytes, and TCP standards work continues. None of these mechanisms guarantees a fixed adoption speed.

link.title: The QUIC Transport Protocol: Design and Internet-Scale Deployment
